title: How do we write fractions as decimals and read them?
description: Fractions and mixed numbers are written as decimals, and then the number 13.117 is read aloud. The digits after the point are read one by one. Keeko's doubt is that the digits after the point form one number.
teaching_notes: One idea: each fraction goes into its own place after the point, and every digit after the point is read by itself. Watch for students who read the digits after the point as one big number.

source: Write in decimal form and read aloud: (e) 8/100 and 9/10 (f) 5/100 (g) 1/10 (h) 2 1/100, 4 1/10 and 7 7/1000. Then read 13.117.
video_script.why: The child has written quantities named by their places and now writes fractions and mixed numbers as decimals.
video_script.substitution: A fraction goes to the place its bottom number names, and the digits after the point are read one by one.
video_script.anchor: a place value chart with units, a point, tenths, hundredths and thousandths
video_script.wrong_move: reads the digits after the point as one number
video_script.payoff_line: Every digit after the point is read by itself

final_answer.value: (e) 0.98 (f) 0.05 (g) 0.1 (h) 2.01, 4.1 and 7.007; 13.117 is thirteen point one one seven
final_answer.spoken: zero point nine eight, zero point zero five, zero point one, two point zero one, four point one, seven point zero zero seven, and thirteen point one one seven

video_script.fraction_reading: tenths, hundredths and thousandths are said as words
hold_back: (e) 0.98 (f) 0.05 (g) 0.1 (h) 2.01, 4.1 and 7.007; 13.117 is thirteen point one one seven
maths_rules: (h) 2 1/100 = 2.01, 4 1/10 = 4.1, 7 7/1000 = 7.007; read two point zero one, four point one, seven point zero zero seven
13.117 is read thirteen point one one seven
the slip: the digits after the point are separate places, so they are not read as 117
video_script.design: The place value chart stays on the stage; each fraction drops into its place in the working band with zeros in the empty places, and 13.117 is read digit by digit. Keeko's doubt reads the three digits as one number.

beats.on_screen: title card From your book, then (e) 8/100 and 9/10 (f) 5/100 (g) 1/10 (h) 2 1/100, 4 1/10 and 7 7/1000, and a last number 13.117; a question mark in the anchor band

marks.list: the fractions and the last number are written

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about writing fractions in decimal form.
<bookmark mark='list'/>It gives some fractions and three mixed numbers.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Write each in decimal form and read it aloud, then read one last number shown on the board.

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board; Keeko sits beside it as the child
narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a place value chart: units, a point, tenths, hundredths and thousandths

marks.chart: the chart of places is drawn

narration: <bookmark mark='chart'/>Remember the place value chart, with three places after the point.
<bookmark mark='zero'/>Each fraction goes to its own place, and the places in between get zeros.

beats.on_screen: Given: some fractions and mixed numbers, and one decimal to read
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, some fractions and mixed numbers, and one decimal to read.

beats.on_screen: To find: each fraction in decimal form, and how to read each decimal
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to write each fraction in decimal form and read every decimal aloud.

beats.on_screen: Step 1 (e): 9/10 + 8/100 = 0.98, read zero point nine eight

marks.e: 9 drops into tenths and 8 into hundredths

narration: <bookmark mark='e'/>Step one, put nine tenths and eight hundredths in their places.
<bookmark mark='write'/>We write it as zero point nine eight, with zero units before the point.

beats.on_screen: Step 2 (f): 5/100 = 0.05, read zero point zero five; (g): 1/10 = 0.1, read zero point one

marks.f: 5 drops into hundredths and a zero fills tenths
marks.g: 1 drops into tenths and 0.1 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='f'/>Step two, five hundredths has no tenths, so a zero fills the tenths place.
<bookmark mark='write'/>That gives zero point zero five.
<bookmark mark='g'/>One tenth is zero point one, with nothing after the one.

marks.h: the whole numbers stay before the point

narration: <bookmark mark='h'/>Step three, a mixed number keeps its whole number before the point.
<bookmark mark='two'/>Two and one hundredth is two point zero one.
<bookmark mark='four'/>Four and one tenth is four point one.
<bookmark mark='seven'/>Seven and seven thousandths is seven point zero zero seven, with zeros in the tenths and hundredths.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: 13.117: the whole part 13 is read as a number; each digit after the point is read by itself: 1, 1, 7

marks.whole: the 13 before the point is circled
marks.digits: the digits 1, 1 and 7 after the point are marked one by one

narration: <bookmark mark='whole'/>Step four, read the whole part before the point as an ordinary number, thirteen.
<bookmark mark='digits'/>Then read each digit after the point by itself, one, one and seven.

beats.on_screen: Answer: (e) 0.98 (f) 0.05 (g) 0.1 (h) 2.01, 4.1 and 7.007; 13.117 is thirteen point one one seven

marks.first: the first three answers are marked

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Every digit after the point is read by itself.
<bookmark mark='first'/>The first three are zero point nine eight, zero point zero five and zero point one.
<bookmark mark='mixed'/>The mixed numbers are two point zero one, four point one and seven point zero zero seven.
<bookmark mark='last'/>The last number is read thirteen point one one seven.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the place value chart
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: 13.117 read as 13 point 117 is struck out; the chart shows 1, 1 and 7 in separate places

marks.fix: 117 is struck out and the digits sit in tenths, hundredths and thousandths

beats.removed: the single number after the point
narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks it is read thirteen point one hundred and seventeen, because one one seven is a number.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But the digits after the point are separate places. Each digit is read alone, so we say thirteen point one one seven.
